hook: The Lady with the Lamp, who founded modern nursing and fought disease with statistics.

pages.x: Florence Nightingale was born in 1820 in Florence, Italy, to a rich English family on a long tour, and named after the city. Her family expected her to marry well, but at 16 she felt God was calling her to a purpose.
In Athens she rescued a baby owl from some boys, named it Athena, and carried it in her pocket. When it died, she had it stuffed; it is now in the Florence Nightingale Museum in London.
Nursing was then seen as low work, for poor and often drunk women. Her family was horrified, but she trained in Germany, and in 1853 ran a small hospital for women in London.

In 1854, in the Crimean War, she took 38 nurses to the British army hospital at Scutari, near Istanbul. Soldiers lay dying of disease in filth, without blankets or soap. She cleaned the wards, found supplies, and organised proper care.
At night she walked the long wards alone with a lamp, checking on the sick. The soldiers loved her, and one wrote that they would kiss her shadow as it fell on their pillows.
She was a brilliant mathematician. With bold, colourful charts, she showed that far more soldiers died of diseases in dirty hospitals than of wounds in battle.
pages.fx: Her charts persuaded the government to clean up army hospitals and cities, and she became the first woman member of the Royal Statistical Society.

pages.x: In 1860 she founded a school for nurses at St Thomas' Hospital in London, the start of nursing as a trained profession. Her Notes on Nursing became a bestseller.

Ill for much of her later life, she worked from her bed for decades, writing reports on hospitals and on clean water in India. In 1907 she became the first woman given the Order of Merit. She died in 1910, aged 90.
Nightingale founded modern nursing and showed how facts and figures can save lives. International Nurses Day is held on her birthday.
pts: Cleaned up army hospitals and saved thousands of soldiers
A pioneer of statistics and charts
